source: Wei et al. (2022) Chain-of-thought prompting elicits reasoning in large language models
finding: Worked examples with the reasoning shown (eight exemplars) lift math accuracy a lot in the largest model.
numbers: PaLM 540B on GSM8K: standard prompting 17.9%, chain-of-thought 56.9% (+39.0 points).
limits: Emergent with scale. Exemplars were hand written.
agent_relevance: Direct machine analogue of worked-example instruction. A solved example with steps beats a bare answer example.

source: Wei et al. (2022) Chain-of-thought prompting elicits reasoning in large language models (headline)
finding: Eight CoT exemplars on PaLM 540B reached state-of-the-art on GSM8K, above fine-tuned GPT-3 with a verifier.
numbers: Abstract claim; same 56.9% result.
limits: Only for 2022-era models.
agent_relevance: Prompting with worked examples can match training. Our scaffold relies on this route.

source: Kojima et al. (2022) Large language models are zero-shot reasoners
finding: A bare instruction ('think step by step') with no examples also lifts accuracy, but less than hand-written worked examples.
numbers: MultiArith 17.7% to 78.7%; GSM8K 10.4% to 40.7%. Zero-shot CoT stays below few-shot CoT. No gain on one-step tasks (SingleEq, AddSub).
limits: Gain needs multi-step problems. Wording matters.
agent_relevance: Generic reasoning instruction is cheap but weaker than worked examples; gain is task dependent.

source: Min et al. (2022) Rethinking the role of demonstrations: what makes in-context learning work?
finding: Demonstrations help mostly through format, label space and input distribution, not through correct labels.
numbers: Replacing gold labels with random labels barely hurts accuracy across 12 models including GPT-3, on classification and multiple-choice tasks.
quote: ground truth demonstrations are in fact not required
limits: Classification and multiple choice; not multi-step reasoning.
agent_relevance: An example may teach format, not the principle. Do not assume a solved example transfers understanding.

source: Lampinen et al. (2022) Can language models learn from explanations in context?
finding: Adding explanations to few-shot examples helps, tuned explanations help more, and matched control text does not help.
numbers: 40 hard tasks, 5-shot, models up to 280B. Regression: untuned explanations give a modest gain; explanations tuned on a small validation set give substantially larger gain; picking examples and explanations together beats picking examples alone.
limits: Only the largest models benefit. Multiple-choice tasks, 2048-token window.
agent_relevance: Supports the human finding that explained examples beat bare ones.

source: Lampinen et al. (2022) component analysis
finding: Explanations tied to examples are a separate, additive part of the prompt next to instructions.
numbers: Figure 2: each prompt component (instructions, untuned explanations, tuned explanations) has its own estimated added contribution in the 280B model.
limits: Read from figure caption, not a table.
agent_relevance: Prefer explained examples over bare rules.

source: Zhou et al. (2022) Least-to-most prompting enables complex reasoning in large language models
finding: Teaching by sequenced subproblems, easy first, lets the model solve problems harder than its examples.
numbers: SCAN with code-davinci-002: at least 99% with 14 exemplars vs 16% with chain-of-thought.
limits: Largest gains on symbolic and compositional tasks.
agent_relevance: Analogue of scaffolding and sequencing. Code can drive the decomposition and feed answers forward.

source: Zhou et al. (2022) Teaching algorithmic reasoning via in-context learning
finding: Very explicit, step-complete teaching of an algorithm (skills, accumulation, composition, tool use) beats looser rationales.
numbers: Error reduction vs best baseline: about 10x long parity, 9x addition, 5x multiplication, 2x subtraction. Omitting the explicit carry equation made the prompt less detailed and worse.
limits: Narrow arithmetic tasks; long prompts.
agent_relevance: Explicit procedure beats vague hint. Fits fixed, code-checked operators.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Telling a model to review and fix its own answer lowers accuracy once oracle labels are removed.
numbers: Intrinsic self-correction, GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7; CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; HotpotQA 49 to 49 to 43. GPT-3.5 kept its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time; changes went more often right to wrong.
limits: Reasoning tasks, a few prompts. Self-correction can help with external signals.
agent_relevance: Reflection instructions without a check are harmful. Matches guardrails G1 and G2.

source: Huang et al. (2024) oracle-label comparison
finding: Earlier reported self-correction gains come from using the true label to decide when to stop.
numbers: With oracle labels: GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3 (GPT-3.5), 95.5 to 97.5 (GPT-4); CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 89.7; HotpotQA 26.0 to 29.0 and 49.0 to 59.0. Calls: 1 vs 3 vs 5, so equal-budget baselines are needed.
limits: Few benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Always compare to a same-budget baseline in our own bench.

source: Du et al. (2023) Improving factuality and reasoning in language models through multiagent debate
finding: Dialogue between several model copies over rounds beats one agent, one reflection, and majority vote on reasoning tasks.
numbers: Six tasks incl. GSM8K (chart axis 70-90%); debate above single agent and self-reflection; both more agents and more rounds needed. Exact per-condition values not extracted this session.
limits: Same model family debating; correlated errors; cost grows with agents x rounds.
agent_relevance: Analogue of dialogue as a teaching method. Treat as a hint only, since copies share errors (G4).

source: Yasunaga et al. (2023) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Asking the model to recall its own relevant solved examples before solving beats 0-shot CoT and matches hand-written few-shot CoT.
numbers: GSM8K: GPT-3.5-turbo 0-shot 75.0, 0-shot CoT 75.8, 5-shot CoT 76.7, self-generated exemplars 77.8. text-davinci-003: 14.8, 50.3, 54.0, self-generated 61.0. K=1 to 5 exemplars: 76.1 to 77.5 on GSM8K.
limits: Self-generated examples can be wrong; gain depends on model strength.
agent_relevance: Agent can write its own worked examples, but G2 and G3 say check them in code.

source: Chang (2023) Prompting large language models with the Socratic method
finding: Socratic techniques (definition, elenchus, dialectic, maieutics, counterfactual) used as prompt templates, claimed to give more precise answers.
numbers: Qualitative examples with GPT-3 via ChatGPT only. No accuracy numbers, no controls.
limits: Anecdotal, single author. Weak evidence.
agent_relevance: Do not cite as proof that Socratic questioning works for LLMs.

source: Chang (2023) Socratic prompting: intent framing
finding: Stating task goal and user intent before the dialogue seemed to help GPT-3 perform better.
numbers: Observation only; no numbers or control.
limits: Anecdote.
agent_relevance: Cheap to test: prepend task goal and intent, then measure.

source: Macina et al. (2023) MathDial: dialogue tutoring dataset with rich pedagogical properties
finding: Strong LLM problem solvers are poor tutors: they reveal answers early and give wrong feedback.
numbers: 3k tutoring dialogues. As teacher, the model revealed the solution 66% of the time and gave incorrect feedback 59% of the time. Fine-tuning on scaffolding dialogue improved the trade-off between student success and telling.
limits: Student is an LLM simulation, not real learners.
agent_relevance: Solving ability is not teaching ability. Scaffolding moves (focus, probing) should be structured by code.

source: Kestin et al. (2025) AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning, Scientific Reports 15:17458
finding: A GPT-4 tutor with expert step-by-step answers and pedagogy rules beat in-class active learning in a randomized crossover.
numbers: 194 analysed of 233 Harvard physics students. Median post-test 4.5 (N=142) vs 3.5 (N=174); pre-test median 2.75. Median gain more than double. Mann-Whitney z=-5.6. Regression effect 0.63; quantile 0.73-1.3 SD. Median 49 min vs about 60 min. Engagement 4.1 vs 3.6.
limits: One course, one site, ceiling effect, no retention test, self-reported engagement. A system prompt alone did not keep multi-part problems in order; expert answers were supplied.
agent_relevance: Pedagogy rules plus a worked reference solution made the tutor work.

source: Bastani et al. (2025) Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning, PNAS 122
finding: Free GPT-4 access boosts practice scores but harms later unaided exams; teacher-designed hints remove most of the harm.
numbers: Nearly 1000 high school math students. Practice grades +48% (GPT Base) and +127% (GPT Tutor). Later exam without AI: -17% for GPT Base; largely mitigated for GPT Tutor.
limits: One school, math, one field experiment.
agent_relevance: Answer-giving instruction creates dependence. Hints instead of answers matter for any agent learning from lessons.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: language agents with verbal reinforcement learning
finding: Agent writes a verbal lesson after failure and reads it on the next trial (feedback and mentoring analogue).
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 91% vs GPT-4 80%. Gains rely on an external signal such as tests.
limits: Huang et al. show gains vanish without external signal on reasoning tasks.
agent_relevance: A lesson is useful only if it cites real output (G2).

source: Zhao et al. (2023) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners
finding: Agent extracts insights from past tries and retrieves successful trajectories; performance rises with experience, no weight updates.
numbers: HotpotQA: ExpeL 40% at round 3 vs Reflexion 39%. Insights-only and trajectory-only modes each help less than both. Tested on HotpotQA, ALFWorld, WebShop, FEVER.
limits: Needs training tasks with success signals.
agent_relevance: Closest agent analogue of instruction from worked examples plus lessons.

source: Liu et al. (2021) What makes good in-context examples for GPT-3?
finding: Which examples you show matters; semantically similar retrieved examples beat random ones.
numbers: Relative gains of 41.9% on ToTTo and 45.5% on Natural Questions over random selection.
limits: Varies by task; fine-tuned encoders do better.
agent_relevance: Retrieve solved examples by similarity, not at random.

source: Rubin et al. (2021) Learning to retrieve prompts for in-context learning
finding: A retriever trained on which examples help the LM beats prior prompt-retrieval methods.
numbers: Substantially above prior baselines on three semantic parsing tasks; exact points not extracted.
limits: Needs annotated data.
agent_relevance: Choose worked examples by measured usefulness.

source: Liu et al. (2023) Lost in the middle: how language models use long contexts
finding: Position of useful information in a long prompt gives a U-shaped accuracy curve; the middle is used worst.
numbers: Multi-document QA, 10-30 documents: best at start or end; with the answer in the middle gpt-3.5-turbo can fall below its closed-book 56.1%.
limits: 2023-era models; newer long-context models improved.
agent_relevance: Put lessons and worked examples at the start or end of the prompt, and keep them few.

source: Critical-Questions-of-Thought (CQoT) (2024)
finding: A pipeline making the model answer critical questions from argumentation theory before answering raised MT-Bench scores.
numbers: MT-Bench Reasoning means (1-10), baseline / step1+4 / CQoT: 8.05 / 8.3 / 8.4 for one model; 6.75 / 6.85 / 7.3 for another. Math: 8.95 / 9.25 / 9.55 and 8.75 / 9.0 / 9.15. Best or joint best in 19 of 20 tests (5 models, 2 domains, vs baseline and CoT).
limits: 80-query benchmark, LLM-judge scores; Sonnet 3.5 tied CoT on math; Nemotron-51b worse than CoT on reasoning.
agent_relevance: Direct critical-thinking-instruction analogue in an LLM loop. Gains modest; judge bias possible (G5).

source: Critical-Questions-of-Thought (CQoT) mechanism
finding: A conclusion is ruled out unless a majority of the critical questions are answered positively.
numbers: Rule: majority of critical questions must pass. Automated as a Python class.
limits: Questions generated by the same model; correlated errors.
agent_relevance: Code can enforce the majority-of-questions gate (G5).

source: Macina et al. (2023) MathDial teacher moves
finding: Human teachers scaffolding an LLM student used Focus questions most and Telling least.
numbers: Focus moves in 37% of teacher utterances; Telling was the rarest move; about 80% of simulated student confusions were conceptual, about a fifth arithmetic.
limits: Teachers were crowd workers; student is simulated.
agent_relevance: Model the scaffold as moves: focus, probe, tell only as last resort.
